title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services

reading.body:
Scammers used AI-generated videos and fabricated social media profiles to impersonate a real, named immigration attorney, then directed victims to pay for fraudulent legal services through consumer payment apps. The failure here is impersonation at scale, made possible by tools that can synthesize a real person's likeness and automate the creation of hundreds of fake accounts across multiple platforms. The fraud operated entirely outside any system the attorney controlled, meaning the deployment point was social media infrastructure, not a legal or AI product he offered.

The platforms were not able to prevent the accounts from appearing in the first place, and removal required a third-party anti-piracy contractor working reactively after harm had begun. No platform-side automated detection caught the pattern before thousands of accounts had already been created and used. A proactive check, such as matching newly created accounts against known professional identities or flagging coordinated inauthentic behavior earlier, might have reduced the window of exposure.

It is not established who the scammers are, whether any victims have recovered money, or whether the payment platforms had any mechanism to flag the transactions as potentially fraudulent.

reports.title: Scammers steal identity of renowned Miami attorney to target immigrants on social media
South Florida immigration attorney says AI scammers are using his identity to target immigrants
Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
Legal resident loses thousands seeking citizenship to AI immigration attorney

summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of an elaborate AI-driven scam targeting vulnerable immigrants. Criminals have created hundreds of fake social media profiles and AI-generated videos using his image to promote fraudulent immigration services, including offers of US residency for $2,200. The scheme escalated dramatically over the past three months after Leal first noticed suspicious activity last October, with scammers directing victims through WhatsApp to send money via payment apps like Venmo and Zelle.

To combat the fraud, Leal hired an online anti-piracy company that has successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake accounts, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram. The scams typically feature fake testimonials from supposed clients or false claims about immigration detention center services. Leal has changed his personal phone number and plans to contact local and federal authorities this week to investigate the scheme. He warns immigrants to verify the identity of anyone offering legal services online and to avoid anyone requesting immediate payment through digital payment platforms.
